catalog_quote: The language has no contrastive stress, but root-final syllables are prosodically most prominent (§4.2.5). ... 4.2.5. Final-syllable prominence In this section it is argued that final syllables of the phonological word are most prominent in terms of showing the maximal degree of phonological contrasts (§4.2.5.1), they tend to have greater phonetic vowel duration than non-final syllables (§4.2.5.2), and excluding a few exceptional cases, their vowels are the most diachronically stable, which means they are the least likely to be syncopated (§4.2.5.3). ... Stated another way, contrast is greatest at the end of the word, either in the final syllable, or on the final two moras in the case of tone. Maximal contrast is one manifestation of a larger pattern of final-syllable prominence. ... an example like this might make it appear as if the language had rhythmic stress manifested as duration.…

sources.citation: Campbell, Eric. 2013. The internal diversification and subgrouping of Chatino. International Journal of American Linguistics 79(3): 395-420. doi:10.1086/670924 (author PDF from UCSB page)
sources.quote: p. 400: 'The major phonological changes that occurred from PZn to PZp were the loss of phonemic vowel nasalization and the shift of prominence from root-final to root-initial syllables (Kaufman 1993).' p. 401: '...loss of non-prominent vowels, where prominent vowels are those in root-final syllables. ... ZEN and ZAC conserve nearly all non-prominent syllables, including those of aspect prefixes.' fn. 10 (p. 402): 'in Zapotec prominence falls on the initial syllable of roots, the opposite of Chatino and PZn (Kaufman 1993).'
sources.note: Same author's comparative statement that Chatino prominence is root-final (pp. 400-402); independent cross-check of the dissertation's §4.2.5 and of the 'pan-Chatino' claim in §4.2.5.4. downloaded and read: confirms.
